Neralu Mobility: Nine Days, Seven Variants

What a product organisation gives up when it cannot have cost, quality and time — and whether those are the only three things on the table.

1. Sunday Night, Cooke Town

At twenty past eleven on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Anuradha Kamath sat at her dining table in Cooke Town, Bengaluru, two laptops open and a third closed beside a cold plate of rice. On the left screen was a spreadsheet her embedded-systems team had rebuilt four times in six days. On the right was a letter from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, forwarded by the Automotive Research Association of India, asking Neralu Mobility Private Limited and two of its customers for a defect report and a corrective action plan by 30 November. The closed laptop held a photograph a fleet supervisor in Mangaluru had sent on 21 October: a cargo three-wheeler on its side outside a Kudla Junction warehouse, the battery enclosure blackened, a rider's helmet on the tarmac. The rider had been treated for burns and discharged the same evening. Kamath had looked at it perhaps forty times since.

At nine the next morning she would sit in Neralu's Domlur office with the chief executive, the chief revenue officer dialling in from New Jersey, the chief financial officer and her engineering and quality leaders, and say which of three paths the company was taking. She was the accountable officer named in the draft filing. She was also, though nobody would say it aloud, the person who in September 2024 had approved the pause that left three of Neralu's seven firmware variants half-migrated — the largest single reason the arithmetic on her left-hand screen would not close.

What she had not worked out was whether the three paths in front of her were actually the three paths, or merely the three that ten days of argument had made easy to see.

2. The Company, and the Decision That Still Binds It

Neralu Mobility was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Kamath and two colleagues from a Hosur electronics supplier, on the bet that India's electric two- and three-wheeler makers would not want to build vehicle software themselves. Neralu made no vehicles. It made the stack that ran inside and around them: the battery management firmware that decided how fast a pack could be charged and when a cell group was misbehaving, the vehicle control unit software, the over-the-air update service, the telematics cloud, and the rider and driver applications. By FY26 it sold that stack to four Indian original equipment manufacturers and three large fleet operators, ran on roughly 3.1 lakh vehicles, and reported revenue of ₹438 crore with EBITDA of ₹31 crore. Of its 1,240 employees, 470 were in engineering: firmware in Bengaluru and Pune, cloud and data in Bengaluru and Toronto, design in Berlin after a small 2023 acquisition, customer success in Singapore, enterprise sales out of New Jersey.

The decision that shaped everything happened in March 2021. Neralu was competing for its first volume contract, with Chilume Motors, a Pune two-wheeler maker preparing its first mass-market scooter. Chilume wanted control over charge curves, thermal thresholds and diagnostics semantics; Neralu's platform offered configuration, not control. Under a fourteen-week deadline, the founders forked the firmware and handed Chilume a dedicated branch. They won the contract, then did the same for the next customer, and the one after that. By 2023 Neralu maintained five distinct firmware lines; a defect found in one had to be ported, rebuilt and revalidated in each of the others, at a cost that grew with every release.

In February 2024 Kamath started Project Sanchaya to collapse the estate into one configurable core, the v5 line, budgeting eighteen months. In September 2024, with a customer launch slipping and a Series C tranche conditioned on it, she paused Sanchaya at about sixty per cent and moved fourteen engineers onto the launch. It was never restarted. Three product lines were left as hybrids: a v5 core with substantial v4 code still resident in the safety path, carrying the divergence of both. Exhibit 2 shows that estate on 15 November 2026.

3. The Industry Around Her

India's electric two-wheeler market had by 2026 settled into an uneasy maturity. Ola Electric, TVS, Bajaj, Ather Energy, Hero's Vida and Greaves' Ampere took most registrations, and the centre of gravity had shifted from early adopters to commercial buyers: last-mile fleets running for Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Flipkart and Amazon India, and cargo three-wheelers competing with the diesel fleets that still moved most urban freight. Those buyers did not care about acceleration. They cared about uptime, kilometres per rupee and depot turnaround between shifts, which had pushed the industry towards higher-rate charging and denser packs.

Regulation had tightened in parallel. After the vehicle fires of 2022 the AIS-156 battery safety standard was amended twice, and homologation through ARAI and ICAT became slower and more literal. The Central Motor Vehicles (Recall) Rules gave manufacturers a route to a voluntary recall and the Ministry the power to order one; a defect on a model supported under PM E-DRIVE could put subsidy eligibility in question, which mattered enormously to Neralu's OEM customers even though Neralu drew no subsidy itself. Telematics brought a second regulator into the room: under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, Neralu's fleet customers had implemented per-vehicle consent for location and behaviour logging, and a meaningful share of vehicles ran with telemetry restricted or coarsely sampled. That consent architecture, built carefully and correctly, was about to matter in a way nobody had planned for.

Neralu's exposure was not only Indian. In March 2026 it had signed Al Rifa Fleet Services LLC of Dubai, running 6,200 electric two- and three-wheelers across Dubai and Sharjah, at ₹38 crore a year with an uptime service level and a sixty-day termination right. Dubai's temperatures from May to September sat where Neralu's bench had never tested.

Compiled from Neralu's programme records and the ARAI correspondence of 9 November 2026. The August 2025 marker is the first cluster of thermal-warning shutdowns, classified at the time as a cell supplier issue and closed.

4. What Happened, and What Turned Out to Be Wrong

In January 2025 two OEM customers qualified a second cell supplier, known internally as Supplier B, at roughly ₹640 per kilowatt-hour less than the incumbent. Neralu's firmware team updated the pack characterisation tables and signed off. In August 2025 eleven thermal-warning shutdowns appeared in the telematics feed from Coimbatore and Hosur, all on Supplier B packs charging on 3.3 kW depot chargers in the afternoon. The firmware team's two-paragraph note concluded that the cells' internal resistance rose faster with temperature than the datasheet implied and that the protection logic had correctly shut the pack down. The ticket was closed as working as designed. Nobody asked the obvious next question, which was whether the protection logic had shut down late.

Through 2026 the events continued at a low rate, as Exhibit 3 shows. On 12 September a cargo three-wheeler burned overnight on charge in a Hosur depot; no one was hurt, and the depot charger was found to have a damaged contactor, which gave everyone a satisfying explanation. On 21 October a second vehicle burned in Mangaluru, in service, forty minutes after a fast charge, with a rider on it. There was no damaged charger. A Kannada news channel ran the footage; two national outlets picked it up next day.

On 3 November a four-person team in Pune produced a root cause the September note had made impossible to see. Neralu's cell-group temperature estimate fused six sensors and a thermal model, smoothed over a rolling eight-second window introduced in 2022 to stop nuisance shutdowns from sensor noise. On Supplier B packs, at states of charge between 62 and 78 per cent, above roughly 38 degrees ambient, with charge currents above 2.6C, one cell group could rise faster than the window could follow. The firmware would permit full charge current for four to nine seconds after the true temperature crossed the taper threshold. It was not, in most cases, enough to cause a fire. It was, the team believed, enough to accelerate degradation in a way that made a later fire more likely — a far harder thing to prove and an even harder thing to file.

Three beliefs that had been load-bearing for a year failed at once. The first was that the telemetry saw everything: Exhibits 3 and 5 do not agree, and the gap is not noise. The second was that the hybrid v5 variants carried v5's regression coverage; Girish Pai's team had measured safety-path coverage at about sixty per cent in June and had not escalated it. The third was that a firmware fix was a firmware fix: because the estimator lived in seven states of divergence, the correction was seven corrections, each with its own validation and, for two, its own homologation question.

5. The People

Anuradha Kamath — Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru

Forty-four, an alumna of NIT Surathkal, at Neralu since she co-founded it. She holds that the company must produce a plan it can defend line by line rather than a fast gesture. Her incentive is uncomfortable: her name is on the ARAI filing, and she carries the platform roadmap any expensive option would consume. What she has not said to anyone, including the chief executive, is that she believes the 2024 pause of Sanchaya was the wrong call and that she would make the same call again under the same tranche conditions.

Girish Pai — Vice President, Embedded Engineering, Bengaluru

From Udupi, eleven years in automotive firmware, three at Neralu. He argues for the complete fix, validated across all seven variants, and for telling the Ministry it will take until February. A bad over-the-air release lands on his organisation, and he has lost three senior firmware engineers to a Chennai OEM this quarter, their notice periods ending 5 December. He has not told the leadership team that safety-path regression coverage on the hybrid variants has been measured at sixty per cent since June, nor that he has quietly moved his best two engineers to the Al Rifa variant because he expects the Gulf summer to be where this breaks next.

Shalini Rao — Director, Quality and Homologation, Pune

Fifteen years in the industry, the only person at Neralu who has sat across a table from ARAI's testing engineers. She wants Neralu to recommend a voluntary recall to its OEM customers: a recall the company proposes is survivable, one the Ministry orders is not. Her signature goes on the submission. What she has not put in writing is a phone call of 11 November, in which a contact at ARAI mentioned that the re-certification queue for amended battery management software would run five to seven weeks through December and January regardless of Neralu's readiness — partly because it was a phone call, partly because writing it down would make one of the options on the table look considerably worse.

Dhruv Mehrotra — Chief Revenue Officer, New Jersey

Joined in 2024 from an enterprise software company; holds the OEM and Gulf accounts and the Series D narrative. He wants a mitigation release inside nine days that demonstrates control to customers and the Ministry, with the deeper work done afterwards. His incentives are the Al Rifa renewal, a variable component tied to net revenue retention, and a term sheet in diligence at a valuation priced on this year's margin. What he has not disclosed is that on 5 November he told Al Rifa's chief operating officer a fix was "days away, not weeks."

Ritu Banerjee — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto

Built the anomaly detection behind Exhibit 3. She holds that nobody yet knows how large the affected population is, that Exhibit 2's scoping comes from a registry lagging service replacements by a quarter, and that two more weeks of instrumented data would change the scope of any fix materially. Her incentive is her model's standing. What she has not repeated loudly is that in June she left a comment on a pull request noting that the fifteen-minute default sampling interval would not capture a thermal transient, closed with the note "cost — revisit in v5."

Nandita Shenoy — Director, Customer Success, Singapore

Covers the Gulf and South-East Asian fleet accounts and, by accident of time zones, relays most bad news. Whatever Neralu decides, she argues, every customer must hear it in the same week and the same words. Her incentive is a retention target and seven operations directors who talk to each other. What she has not told the leadership team is that two Indian fleet customers have formally requested the raw telematics data their contracts entitle them to, which will show them the same discrepancy between Exhibits 3 and 5 that Neralu is currently arguing about internally.

Lars Hoffmann — Design Director, Berlin

Owns the rider and fleet-manager applications. If Neralu caps charging rate, he argues, riders must be told in the app why their vehicle now takes longer, since they will otherwise conclude the battery is failing. His incentive is a design organisation that has spent a year arguing for candour. What he has not said is that the disclosure flow cannot be localised into Arabic, Kannada, Tamil and Marathi and cleared through app store review in nine days, so the first fortnight of "transparent disclosure" would reach English readers only.

Tariq Al Rifa — Chief Operating Officer, Al Rifa Fleet Services, Dubai

Runs 6,200 vehicles on contracts with their own delivery windows. Neither a slow fix nor a charge-rate cap is acceptable to him; Neralu, he says, should bear the cost of replacing cells and chargers on his fleet. His incentive is a summer from April in which a cap would cost him roughly one shift in six. What he has not told Neralu is that since September he has been running a competitor's stack on 300 vehicles in Sharjah.

7. Voices

8. The Options as Kamath Currently Sees Them

The first path is to do the whole job. Correct the estimator in the v5-C core, port it to all seven variants, run full regression on each, re-certify the two variants whose safety path is materially altered, and tell the Ministry on 30 November that corrective action completes by mid-February. Exhibit 2 puts validation at 64 bench-days across four benches; Pai's estimate, allowing for the 5 December resignations, is eleven to fourteen weeks. It yields on time. What the framing hides is that through those weeks 41,800 vehicles — or 69,000, or some number Banerjee cannot yet give — keep running the defective estimator into a Gulf spring, so the option that appears to protect quality also leaves the most vehicles unfixed the longest.

The second path is the mitigation. A small change caps charge current at 1.8C whenever estimated ambient exceeds 34 degrees, removing the trigger condition without repairing the estimator. It touches the same code path, can be validated on a reduced regression suite and a 400-vehicle pilot, and can plausibly reach the field by 24 November. It costs almost nothing in rupees. It yields on quality — not on the safety outcome, which it probably improves, but on the evidence that it has improved, which is what a regulator and two OEM customers will be reading. It also degrades what the customer paid for: depot turnaround, a shift in six to Al Rifa from April and a visible slowdown for every Indian fleet from March. And it leaves the estimator wrong.

The third path is to buy the way out: a Pune validation house at ₹4.5 crore, three more hardware-in-the-loop benches at ₹6.2 crore on an eight-week lead time a supplier will compress to three for a premium, retention packages for the departing engineers, and Toronto re-scoping with 1 Hz logging on a consented subset. Finance puts the package at ₹18.5 crore against FY27 EBITDA guidance of ₹31 crore. It yields on cost. The uncomfortable part is that the two scarcest inputs cannot be bought inside the window: ARAI's queue, and engineers who already know 31,600 lines of divergence in the v5-H1 safety path.

Kamath had written the three paths on a sheet of paper on Thursday and could not stop noticing what it left out. Nowhere on it was how many vehicles, which Exhibit 2 answers with a confidence Exhibit 5 does not support and which, if the answer were 12,000 rather than 41,800, would let the first path finish before Christmas. Nowhere on it was which variants, although v5-C, the one variant nobody had forked, needed five bench-days and had no affected vehicles at all. And nowhere on it was the possibility that the honest plan to file on 30 November was not a fix but a programme — the one she had paused in September 2024.

9. The Deadline and the Hard Edges

Four constraints were not negotiable by Monday morning. The Ministry's letter required a defect report and corrective action plan by 30 November; Rao's reading was that a plan with dates the company then missed would be worse than a longer plan honestly stated, though she conceded she had never tested that. The Al Rifa contract carried a 97 per cent availability service level with a ₹40 lakh monthly penalty below it and a sixty-day termination for cause, and a charge cap would move availability by more than three points in a Gulf summer. The Chilume master agreement capped Neralu's software-defect indemnity at ₹12 crore but let Chilume withhold thirty per cent of quarterly fees pending resolution of a Class A defect — on ₹96 crore a year, some ₹7.2 crore a quarter of cash. And Series D diligence closed on 18 December, on an FY27 EBITDA number that ₹18.5 crore of unplanned spend would not survive intact.

Against those sat the softer constraints that would decide the outcome. Three senior firmware engineers left on 5 December. Two of four benches could not run the v5 hybrids. Berlin was on holiday from 22 December. And the Indian fleets, unlike Al Rifa, were entering their best quarter, with wedding-season and quick-commerce volumes running depots at capacity through January.

10. Questions for Discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 2, 3 and 5 together, what is your best estimate of the affected population, and how much does each path depend on that estimate being right?
  2. Exhibit 4 appears to show that risk declines above 38 degrees. What would you need to believe for that reading to be true, and what does the exhibit's footnote do to that belief?
  3. The first path is described inside Neralu as "not compromising on quality." Whose quality does it protect, and whose does it spend? Answer for a rider in Mangaluru, a depot manager in Sharjah and an ARAI testing engineer in Pune.
  4. Neralu has yielded on quality twice before — the 2021 fork and the 2024 pause — each time to protect a date. What did those trades cost, and where in Exhibit 2 is the invoice?
  5. Scope is not one of Kamath's three paths. Construct an option that yields primarily on scope, say what it gives up, and explain why no one has proposed it.
  6. You are Kamath at nine o'clock on Monday morning. Which one of cost, quality and time do you yield, and how do you say so in a single sentence to your leadership team? What then goes into the corrective action plan on 30 November, and what do you tell the board on 18 December about the one you gave up?

It was past one when she closed the spreadsheet. She had written and deleted Monday's opening line four times. The version she disliked least was we are going to be worse at one of these three things on purpose, and I am going to tell you which one, and she could not decide whether that was leadership or a way of avoiding the harder sentence underneath: that Neralu had been worse at all three, quietly, for five years, and had called it velocity. Outside, the last Deepavali lights hung unlit across the neighbour's balcony. Her phone showed a message from Nandita Shenoy in Singapore, sent nine minutes earlier, where it was already Monday: Tariq's office has asked for a call at 10 a.m. Gulf time. What do I tell them we are doing?

Sharavathi Systems: The October 1 Deadline

A short decision case on cost, quality and time trade-offs in engineering delivery

1. The Scene

At a quarter past nine on the morning of 15 September 2026, Deepak Hegde stood at the window of Sharavathi Systems' fourth-floor office on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road, watching the Sarjapur traffic congeal below, and rehearsed the number he would have to say out loud in forty-five minutes. Hegde, thirty-eight, was Vice President of Engineering at Sharavathi, a mandate-and-recurring-payments infrastructure company that eleven Indian banks and three large NBFCs relied on to process standing instructions, SIP debits, insurance premiums and subscription payments. He was due in a leadership call with Sharavathi's CEO, its sales head and its largest client's representative in Dubai, to say which of three imperfect paths engineering would take to meet a Reserve Bank of India compliance deadline that fell, immovably, on 1 October. The team was not going to finish everything, on time, at the standard of testing Hegde considered safe. Something had to give. His job that morning was to say plainly what, and why.

2. Company Background

Sharavathi Systems was founded in 2016 by two former engineers from a large private bank's payments division, on the simple observation that Indian banks were bad at building recurring-payment plumbing themselves and worse at maintaining it. The company built application programming interfaces that sat between a bank's core banking system and the National Payments Corporation of India's mandate rails, letting a bank or an NBFC register, execute and reconcile e-mandates and NACH debits without building that machinery in-house. By 2026 Sharavathi processed roughly 42 crore recurring debit instructions a month across fourteen bank and NBFC partners, on a revenue run rate of about ₹210 crore a year. Its competitors were payments majors with adjacent subscription products — Razorpay, Cashfree Payments and Juspay — but Sharavathi's pitch to banks was narrower: compliance-grade mandate infrastructure, nothing else, built by a team that did nothing but track RBI's payments circulars for a living. The company had raised a Series C round in 2024 and employed about 340 people, with an engineering organisation of ninety split across Bengaluru and Pune, a product design function anchored in Berlin since an acquihire in 2023, a data science team of six in Toronto that built the fraud and risk models embedded in the mandate engine, and commercial teams in Singapore and New Jersey serving Sharavathi's expansion into Gulf-linked NRI remittance products.

3. The Situation

In August 2026, RBI had issued a circular extending its additional-factor-authentication requirement for e-mandates to cover recurring debits between ₹1 and ₹5,000 — a band that had, since the 2019 framework, been exempt from the extra authentication step precisely because it covered small, high-frequency payments like OTT subscriptions and SIP instalments. The circular set 1 October 2026 as the compliance date, with no stated provision for a phased or partner-by-partner extension: from that date, any bank or NBFC found processing exempt-band mandates without the new authentication and pre-debit notification workflow would be required to suspend new mandate registrations on its platform until it recertified. For Sharavathi, this meant rebuilding and re-certifying the authentication workflow across all fourteen of its bank partners' individual technical integrations, since each partner's core banking system spoke to Sharavathi's mandate engine slightly differently.

By 15 September, Kavya Shastri, the engineering manager leading the compliance workstream from Bengaluru, had the core workflow built and functioning end-to-end for the company's six largest bank partners, who together carried 88% of Sharavathi's mandate volume. Full regression testing, load testing and RBI-style certification sign-off — the standard Sharavathi applied before any change touched live bank rails — was complete for four of those six. For the remaining eight partners, smaller regional banks and NBFCs carrying the last 12% of volume, the workflow was built but essentially untested; Arjun Deshmukh, the Pune-based staff engineer who owned partner integrations, estimated five to seven working days of dedicated testing per partner to reach the same certification standard, and the team could not run those in parallel without pulling engineers off the six-partner path that was already tight. From Toronto, data scientist Wei Chen had flagged a separate concern: the fraud-scoring rules that decided which transactions needed the new authentication step had been tuned on the large partners' data only, and applying them un-recalibrated to the smaller partners' transaction patterns risked false declines during the October festive season, when SIP and insurance debit volumes typically rose by a third around Dussehra and Diwali. From Singapore, customer success lead Meera Iyer was already fielding early questions from partner banks about downtime windows, and from Dubai, Sharavathi's largest single client by fee revenue — Al Fahd Digital Bank, which used Sharavathi's rails for NRI-linked recurring remittance-adjacent payments into India — sat in the tail group of eight, unhappily.

4. The People

Kavya Shastri, Engineering Manager, Bengaluru, had led the compliance build since July and wanted, above all, to avoid a repeat of February 2026, when a rushed fraud-rule change had caused a weekend of failed debits at two partner banks and cost Sharavathi roughly ₹60 lakh in reconciliation work and goodwill credits. She argued for protecting the testing bar even if it meant some partners went live late.

Rohan Mehta, Head of Sales for the Americas and Gulf accounts, New Jersey, had Al Fahd Digital Bank's renewal, worth roughly ₹9 crore a year, coming up for signature in November, and worried that any visible sign that Sharavathi could not hit a regulator's date for a marquee client would colour that renewal conversation badly, whatever the underlying engineering logic.

Meera Iyer, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, spoke daily with partner banks' operations teams and wanted, more than a particular technical outcome, an honest and early answer she could relay to all fourteen partners at once rather than partner-by-partner bad news arriving in dribs over the following fortnight.

Youssef Al Marri, Head of Payments at Al Fahd Digital Bank, Dubai, wanted his bank's mandate registrations to keep functioning without interruption from 1 October, and was less interested in Sharavathi's internal trade-offs than in a specific, credible date by which his bank's workflow would be certified.

6. The Options

Option A — Hit the date for everyone, yield on quality

Sharavathi could ship the new authentication workflow to all fourteen partners on 1 October, including the eight untested Tier 3 partners, relying on close production monitoring rather than full pre-launch regression and load testing to catch problems. This protected the relationship with every partner, including Al Fahd, and cost nothing extra. Its evident risk was a repeat of February's incident, this time during the highest-volume weeks of the year, at partners least equipped to absorb a reconciliation mess.

Option B — Protect quality and cost, yield on time for the tail

Sharavathi could certify the six largest partners, covering 88% of volume, by 1 October, and tell the remaining eight, including Al Fahd, that their workflow would be tested and certified in phases through October, with each partner's new mandate registrations frozen until its own certification was complete. This kept the testing bar Kavya Shastri wanted and added no direct cost, but meant Sharavathi delivering, to a client renewing at ₹9 crore a year, the news that his bank alone among Sharavathi's mandate partners would not be compliant on the regulator's date.

Option C — Protect quality and time, yield on cost

Sharavathi could bring in a Pune-based testing vendor and short-term contractors, and pay the Bengaluru and Pune teams weekend allowances, to complete full testing and certification for all fourteen partners by 1 October, at a cost of roughly ₹45 lakh. This was the only option that avoided both a quality compromise and a partner-facing delay, but it assumed unfamiliar contractors could become productive on a compliance-critical codebase within five working days, an assumption Arjun Deshmukh in Pune was not confident of.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 tell you about why finishing "everything" by 1 October was disproportionately harder than the 88% completion figure suggests?
  2. Whose interests does each option protect, and whose does it put at risk — Kavya Shastri's engineering standard, Rohan Mehta's renewal, or Meera Iyer's relationship with all fourteen partners equally?
  3. Is the risk in Option A genuinely comparable across a small NBFC partner and a strategic client like Al Fahd Digital Bank, or does Exhibit 2's single risk estimate hide an important difference between partners?
  4. If you were Deepak Hegde, which of cost, quality or time would you choose to yield on, and what would you say to Youssef Al Marri in Dubai to justify that choice?

8. A Note for the Learner

The cost–quality–time triangle is not a diagram to admire; it is a discipline for moments exactly like this one. The mistake Hegde had to avoid was not choosing badly — it was failing to choose at all, and instead letting the organisation quietly erode all three at once: a bit less testing here, a bit of slipped scope there, a bit of unplanned overtime everywhere, with no one able to say afterward what had actually been traded for what. The topic's lesson is that when a team is behind, exactly one of the three should give, deliberately and visibly, while the other two are actively defended.

Applied here, Option A quietly sacrifices quality while claiming to protect both time and cost — which is the least defensible kind of trade-off, because the cost of the quality failure (a repeat ₹60-lakh incident, at higher volume, at the regulator's own compliance deadline) is real but deferred and uncertain, which is exactly the kind of cost organisations are worst at weighing against a certain, immediate deadline. Option C is the cleanest trade on paper — it protects both quality and time by spending money — but it rests on an assumption, contractor productivity within five days on compliance-critical code, that Sharavathi's own staff engineer doubted, so the "cost" column in Exhibit 2 likely understates the option's true price.

The most defensible path is Option B: certify the 88% of volume that can be certified properly by the deadline, and say plainly, to RBI's spirit if not its letter, to Rohan Mehta, and to Youssef Al Marri directly, that the remaining partners will be phased in over October with new-mandate registrations paused rather than run on undertested code. This is defensible because it names its trade-off honestly — time, for a clearly bounded and communicated group of partners — rather than hiding a quality trade behind a confident delivery date, or a cost trade behind an unverified contractor plan. It also converts an abstract risk into a concrete, manageable one: a paused registration queue at eight partners is inconvenient and commercially uncomfortable, but it is bounded and visible, where a production incident during Diwali week is neither. The harder part of Option B is not the engineering; it is Hegde's conversation with Al Marri, which is where a well-reasoned technical decision either earns trust because it was made in the open, or loses it because it was announced too late to matter.
